Australia’s international aid
In 2007–8, some of the top recipient countries of Australian government aid were:
• Papua New Guinea – $355.9 m 
 
• Solomon Islands – $95.4 m
• Indonesia – $179.1 m 
 
 
• Vietnam – $73.7 m
• East Timor – $72.8 m 
 
 
• Philippines – $89.9 m
• Cambodia – $33 m  
 
 
• China – $30 m
1 Describe the spatial distribution of these countries in relation to Australia.
 
 
 
 
2 Suggest reasons why these countries are some of the top recipients of Australia’s aid.
 
 
 
 
People often say: ‘Give a man a fish and you feed him for a day, teach a man to fish and you feed him for a 
lifetime.’ The quote below is from Oxfam Community Aid Abroad’s Submission to the Human Rights  
Sub-Committee of the Joint Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs Defence and Trade ‘The link between aid 
and human rights’.
The sentiments of Thin, a woman leader from Check village, Takeo Province, Cambodia:
A man is just as likely to be a woman, and she already knows how to fish.
She would like her river left alone by illegal logging companies or fish poachers using dynamite  
and working in collusion with corrupt local government officials.
She would prefer that her government did not build huge dams with the help of the Asian 
Development Bank, dams that have reduced fish stocks dramatically and damaged her livelihood.
She would prefer that police did not use violence to enforce mass evictions to enable the dams  
to be built.
She doesn’t want charity.
She would like her basic rights respected.
International aid is complex – it is not simply a case of giving money to poorer countries and expecting their 
standards of living to start improving.
The challenge is to provide aid in appropriate, effective and culturally sensitive ways.
3 How can this be achieved?

Australia and migration

to, but because they choose to. The movement of people out of a country is known as emigration. Some 
people emigrate from Australia, but many more migrate here. Together, migrants have created huge 
economic and social change in this country.

The Australian wine industry
The Australian wine industry has grown considerably over the past few decades. Today, Australian wines are 
exported to 80 countries around the world. In 2006, around 1.85 million tonnes of grapes were crushed by 
Australian wine-makers. In 2005–6, the Australian wine industry exported 722 million litres of wine, worth 
$2.7 billion. Nearly two-thirds was red wine.
The top five overseas markets for Australian wine in 2005–6 were:
•  UK (34%)     •  USA (31%)     •  Canada (9%)     •  NZ (3%)      •  Netherlands (2%)
A record volume of wine was also sold domestically in that year – 431 million litres.

Drought in Australia
Meteorologists monitor and measure drought severity in terms of rainfall deficiencies for different regions. 
Research has shown that severe drought affects some part of Australia on average once in 18 years. 
However, periods between severe droughts have varied between four and 38 years. Because of the variation 
in climate across the country, there is little chance that the entire country would all be drought-affected at 
the same time.

Brazil is the country with the greatest area of untouched tropical rainforest in the world. Between 2000 and

1 Business goals 2

A goal is something that a person, group or business hopes to achieve in the future. Within a business there are three
types of goals: the personal goals of the owner, financial goals and social goals.

Owner’s personal goals

A person who owns a business is called an owner. On a personal level, owners operate a business for two main reasons. First,
independence atlows them to make their own decisions rather than follow or carry out the decisions of another person. Second,
a5 long as the decisions they make are wise, their job will be secure,

Financial goals

Financial goals relate directly to money. One financial goal is profit [Income ~ expenses = profit]. The main financial goal of
businesses, other than non-profit organisations, is to make a profit. For a business to make a profit, generally it must increase
sales and reduce expenses [sales earn a business income].

Another financial goal is business growth. If a business expands—for example, if a second or third store is opened—then more
income will usually be earned.

A third financial goal is that of an increase in market share. Market share refers to the total sales [expressed as a percentage] a
business has experienced in a given market. Most businesses will have an increase in market share as a financial goal because it
directly relates to an increase in sales of a particular product. The final financial goal is return on investment. Return on
investment refers to the expected percentage return that an investment will earn for the business. The larger the percentage, the
more profitable the business.

Social goals

Social goals relate to the community, One such goal, sustainable ecological development, refers to the use of resources by
businesses. This particular goal aims for the sensible use of resources by businesses so that there are enough resources for future
generations of people to use. Another social goal is community service. For example, businesses have a role to play in sponsoring
community events.

2 Costs of running a business 2

The word ‘cost’ means how much money is required to pay for something. People encounter costs on 9 daily basis—for example,
purchasing a bus ticket, a can of softdrink or a magazine. Just as people have a set amount of money to spend, so too do
businesses.

Businesses [except for non-profit organisations} have financial goals of profit. Therefore, to Sessa
increase their profit, businesses must consider costs from day to day. Ps Le puale a .
There are two types of costs: fixed and variable. Fixed costs stay the same over a given period of —rént insurance, WEges,
time—for example, rent, insurance and wages, Rent is the money a business owner pays for Purchasing stock,

Variable costs, on the other hand, change over a period of time. Examples of variable costs include

electricity, transport and telephone. A retail business would spend more per fortnight on
electricity in winter, heating the shop, than it would in spring. Other examples of variable costs
include promotion and transportation.

To calculate whether a business has made a profit the following formula is used: Zy,
PROFIT = INCOME - COSTS (FIXED + VARIABLE) Y

A business that keeps a record of its costs is more likely to succeed than a business that does not. If a business does not keep a
close eye on its costs over an extended period of time, bankruptcy could result, Bankruptcy involves a business ceasing to trade
as a result of being unable to meet its debts of $1500 or more. The person[s) who ran the business cannot legally run a business
for the next three years.

4 Exporting

Business operates on a global scale. The introduction of mew technology and the advancements in transportation allow Australia
to deal with other countries more efficiently. Operating on a global scale allows Australia to export and import a greater variety of
goods and services.

Exporting refers to the process whereby a country sells goods and services to another country, For example, when Australia sells
meat to Japan, Australia is said to be exporting meat.

Australia trades with many foreign countries. During the 1930s, Australia’s traditional connection was with Europe. In particular,
Australia had a close trading partnership with the United Kingdom, Germany and France. These three countries comprised close
to 60 per cent of Australia’s exports.

In recent decades, Australia has forged a trading relationship with Asia-Pacific countries. Countries of the Asia-Pacific region
inctude Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Japan and Thailand. As a direct result, in 1996-97, trade with the European countries
mentioned above only accounted for 7 per cent of Australia’s exports.

Trade with Japan, particularly in the 1980s and 1990s, was of major financial importance to Australia. In 1991-92 exports to Japan
were at their highest, representing 25 per cent of Australia’s total exports. In 1996-97 they slipped to 18 per cent.

5 Stakeholders in a business

A stakeholder is any person or group that has an interest in the operation of a business. A stakeholder has an interest in the
business because they are somehow affected by the way it is run. A stakeholder is different to a shareholder because a
shareholder is a person or business that owns shares in a business. You must remember, however, that a stakeholder can be from
the internal or external business environment.

directly under the control of a business. Examples of internal directly under the control of @ business. Some examples
stakeholders include the employer and the employees. include customers, creditors [people to whom the business

7 GST 2)

what is tax?

Taxation, or tax as it is commonly known, is a voluntary contribution by income earners to the government, People paying tax to
the government allow for the upkeep of infrastructure for the general population. Examples of infrastructure include public roads,
hospitals, schools and the police. The three overriding principles of a tax system should be that it Is simple, fair and neutral.

History behind the GST

The letters GST stand for ‘goods and services tax’. The GST is 3 new tax that was introduced in Australia by the Liberal Government,
under the leadership of Prime Minister John Howard, in 2000, The Liberal-National Party Coalition won the 1999 federal election
with an election platform that featured the GST. Since the majority of the Australian population voted for the Coalition, they also
voted for the GST,

Before the GST became law, there was a lot of debate in parliament and in the media over the finer details of the new tax,
particularly over the issue of whether to tax fresh food. The Liberal Party negotiated with the Democrats, led by Senator Meg Lees,
in order to gain enough votes to ensure the Bill passed through the Senate.

What is the GST?

The GST is a broad-based tax of 10 per cent on most goods and services. It was introduced in Australia on 1 July 2000. Everyone
is subject to the GST, because it is included in the prices of most goods and services. The GST replaced the Wholesale Sales Tax
{sales tax) as the major indirect tax. Sales tax is a tax on the wholesale price of an item. Sales tax was imposed only on the sale of
goods whereas the GST applies to both goods and services. The Federal Government implemented the new tax in order to increase
the ‘base’ upon which revenue could be raised and to reduce the opportunities for people to avoid paying the correct amount of
income tax. The Federal Government made a concession for the GST by reducing personal income tax. At the same time, family
assistance, pensions and allowances were increased.

What items are GST-free?

The following items do not have GST included in their price: basic food, eligible childcare, water and sewerage rates, education,
most health services and products, hospital and nursing home services, and local government rates.

Food and the GST

GST does not increase the price of basic food, the general rule being that fresh or unprocessed food is exempt from the GST.
Replacing sales tax with a 10 per cent GST has meant that the prices of some food items have decreased. Some prices have risen—
for example, takeaway meals and restaurant meals.

Who monitors the prices of goods and services? pe}

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission [ACCC] monitors the prices of goods and services, The Commission plays
an important role in relation to the GST in Australia. Its role is to make sure that prices have been adjusted correctly and that
consumers benetit from the new indirect tax changes. For this reason the ACCC is referred to as the ‘consumer watchdog’.

8 Buying an established business @

I ‘This worksheet involves using the business section of a newspaper.

ACTIVITY 4

It is essential that you understand the language of business before you decide to purchase an already established one. Therefore,
before you decide to purchase your business, look through the business section of a newspaper and write down any abbreviations:
that you do not understand, Try to work out what they stand for. For example, K stands for thousand [in dollars).

ACTIVITY 2

From the newspaper choose three types of business, such as mewsagencies, cafés and restaurants. Write your chosen three
business types as headings in your book. For each of your three chosen business types, answer the following questions:

1 How many businesses are for sale in the category that you have researched?
2 Where are these businesses located? Are they in different suburbs?

2 Is there a difference in the selling price of businesses in the same category? If so, list prices to justify your answer.

4 Suggest reasons why businesses in the same category might be selling at different prices. (Hint: Location and sales.!

Activity 3

Imagine that you could purchase one of the businesses that you have been reading about in the newspaper. Choose one of the
business types that you have read about. Cut out the advertisement and paste it into your book, then answer the following
questions in relation to your chosen business.

1 State the name and location of the business.
2 What is the selling price for the business?
3 List two reasons why you chose to purchase this particular business instead of other businesses listed in the newspaper.

& Asa soon-to-be owner of your chosen business, what five questions would you need to ask before purchasing the established
business?

Polymer is a compound like plastic. Research Austratian polymer currency then, in the spaces

1 What am I?

Jam the smallest of Australian notes (both in size and vatuel. | was released in plastic form in 1992, but my design has since been
changed because | was experiencing problems with my security features. | was recoloured in 1995. My theme is Australian
governing powers. My front features Queen Elizabeth Il, and on my reverse side | have a picture of the Old and New Partiament
Houses in Canberra. Bruce Stewart designed me. | am mauve and pink in colour. In 2001 a new note was released to circulate
alongside me as part of the Centenary of Federation celebrations. It features Sir Henry Parkes, ‘Father of Federation’, on the front,
and Catherine Helen Spence, the first woman to stand for election to public office in Austratia on the back.

2 What am I?

| was the last plastic Australian note to be introduced [1996]. My theme is Australians’ achievements. On my front is a picture of
Dame Nellie Metba [1861-1931]. Melba was a world famous soprano [opera singer}. She adopted her ‘stage’ last name Melba”
because it was an abbreviation of her birth place—Melbourne, During World War |, Melba lived in Australia. It was during this
period of time that she worked to raise money for war charities. On my reverse side is a picture of Sir John Monash (1845-1931).
Monash was a politician, administrator and engineer, He studied engineering and law at the University of Melbourne. During World
War |, Monash was made commander of the 4th Infantry Brigade of the Australian Imperial Force, In the 1920s Monash
represented returned soldiers. Bruce Stewart designed me. | am green and yellow in colour.

3 What am I?

| was introduced in plastic form in 1993. My theme is Australian writers, On my front is a picture of A.B. ‘Banjo’ Paterson
[1866-1941]. Paterson was a poet, batlad writer, journalist and horseman. Paterson is remembered for composing the song
“Waltzing Matilda’ but he is best known as the author of the book The Man from Snowy River and Other Verse. On my reverse side
is a picture of Dame Mary Gilmore [1865-1962]. Gilmore was an author, journalist, poet and tireless campaigner against injustice
‘and deprivation. She wrote under a pseudonym while a teacher so that her work could be published. Gilmore also believed in social
justice and worked for the retief of the poor and the just treatment of Aboriginals. Max Robinson designed me, | am blue, green
and yellow in colour.

Reibey was a pioneer businesswoman with interests in shipping and property. After the death of her husband in 1811, Reibey ran
several business interests. On my reverse side is a picture of Reverend John Flynn (1880-1951). Flynn pioneered the world’s first
aerial medical service, which began operation in 1934. Today, the organisation is known as the Royal Flying Doctor Service of

but lack of funds prevented these inventions from being produced for commercial sale. Unaipon’s article ‘Aboriginals: Their
tradition and customs’ was the first Aboriginal article to be published. On my reverse side is a picture of Edith Cowan [1861-1932].

10 Automatic teller machines

Introduced in Australia in 1981, automatic teller machines [ATMs] are a very common sight these days: outside banks, in nearly
every suburb and shopping centre, and even in petrol stations,

ATMs are a modern convenience for busy people, who can now access their money electronically outside the traditional banking
hours {? am-4 pm, Monday to Fridayl.

An ATM allows consumers to undertake many operations including withdrawing money,
transferring money from one account to another, and finding out the balance of an
account.

Can you think of what an account holder needs to operate an ATM?

If you suggested a PIN (Personal Identification Number] and a plastic card,
then you were right.

A PIN is a numerical code [although sometimes words are used as substitutes for
numbers) that allows the account holder to access money in a specific account. It is very
important to keep the PIN to themselves because it

allows access to their account and therefore their

= a

If the PIN is used incorrectly more than three times,

the ATM will not return the card, This is to prevent an

unauthorised person from trying to gain access to

another person's account. If a person loses their ATM

card they should report it to their bank immediately.

The bank will then proceed with a security check and issue a new card [generally within seven

days].

Once the consumer has withdrawn money from an ATM, they can choose whether to receive a
transaction record [or slip}. The slip of paper has the following details printed on it: the account
number, date of transaction, time of transaction, type and amount of transaction, and available
balance.

The consumer should keep all transaction slips so they can check each ATM transaction
against the next bank statement,

card, cash and receipt in your wallet].

When directly in front of the ATM take your plastic card out of your wallet.

Read the instructions and follow the prompts, The first instruction is to enter your PIN.

If the information you have entered is correct, press the OK button.

11 Create your own money

Congratulations! You entered a competition to design a $50 note.
You competed against ten other finalists in the nationwide money
design competition and WON! Before you present your newly
designed $50 note for printing be sure that your note displays all
the characteristics of money.

You have no doubt learnt about the characteristics of money. You
will then recall that money must be: durable, divisible, portable,
acceptable and scarce.

Second, money has certain security features. Have a close look at t
an Australian note and you will discover the following security

features on it: amount of the note, country of origin, watermark, =
hologram, serial number, detailed background, signature of the

Governor of the Reserve Bank of Australia and the signature of the

Secretary to the Treasurer.

Your task is to write a proposal and create a model of the design
that won the competition.

Imagine if all the money you earned could be spent. Unfortunately, this is not the case for most people. People save money so they
can pay for things in the near future. A person may save in order to purchase additional goods and services. For example, some
people choose to save their money so they can buy a car or a new computer.

14 Needs and wants vs goods and
services

Needs and wants

There are particular items that are required by all people. They are called ‘needs’. A need, also referred to as an essential, is an
item that is necessary for survival, People require needs in order to survive. Water, food, clothing and shelter are essential for a
person's survival.

All other items, besides those categorised as needs, are referred to as wants. A want is not essential for survival. Examples of
wants include CD players, cars, microwaves, computers and tennis rackets. Wants are also called luxury items.

Do you see a change in people's needs with the advancement of modern society? As societies become more technologically
advanced, what was once considered a ‘want’ is mow for some people a ‘need’, Although not essential for basic survival, in
particular occupations a car is considered to be a need. For couriers and taxi drivers, whose job involves driving a motor vehicle
of some type, a car is a modern need.

Goods and services

A good is an item that can be purchased by a consumer. A good is tangible (you can touch it). Examples of a good include a
computer, a car, an iter of clothing and a pen.

When you purchase a good, you often need to purchase an additional good so the original good can function properly. The purchasing
of an additional good is called a complementary good. For example, if you purchase a CD player you also need to purchase a CD.

Goods can also be divided into individual and collective goods. An individual good is an item that is solely for personal use. For
example, Sarah's rollerblades are an individual good. On the other hand, goods that are used by the community are called

collective goods. For example, the local swimming pool is a collective good.

A service is an act performed for a consumer, Unlike a good, a service is intangible lyou cannot touch it, but you can see it being
done}. Examples of a service include work performed by a dentist, hairdresser, teacher and a mechanic.

15 Bankruptcy 2

Bankruptcy is regularly reported in newspapers and on the nightly TV news. But what does bankruptcy mean? The word
‘bankruptcy’ refers to a financial situation where there is legal recognition that a person or a business is no longer able to pay their
debts [money owing]. A person or business must owe at least $1500 to be declared bankrupt, The person/business that owes the
money is called the debtor, The person/business to whom/which the money is owed is called the creditor.

For example, Caitlin [the debtor] is unable to pay Enrico [the creditor] the sum of $53000, Caitlin can either declare herself
bankrupt or it can be done by a creditor. In both cases, bankruptcy must be proven six months before filing for bankruptcy.

In the case of Caitlin, if she is unable to meet her debts, then her financial position should be legally recognised and her assets
controtled by an official. An asset is a valuable that can be sold in order to meet outstanding debts. The assets are handed over to
an official. The role of the official is to divide the assets [converted into cash) equally among creditors. It must be remembered that
although the assets have been converted into cash, not all creditors will be paid in full. Once Caitlin has been declared bankrupt,
her financial status is that of ‘bankrupt’.

Caitlin must remember that this financial state will remain for three years and in that time she cannot obtain credit of more than
$500 and she cannot change her name in order to operate a business. Enrico too must keep in mind that once Caitlin has been
declared bankrupt he cannot try to regain his debt [if not already recovered).

As mentioned above, in order for Caitlin’s debt to be paid, her assets were placed under the direct control of an official. The
Bankruptcy Act 1966 does not allow certain debtor's assets to be sold to pay creditors. Caitlin’s essential clothing, household
property, life assurance policies, income and means of transport (up to $2500 worth] will not be taken away from her.

The five characteristics of money

1 Divisible: People buy goods and services valued at different prices, For this reason, money needs to be available in different
denominations. If a person buys a CD for $20, but hands a $50 note to the salesperson, the customer is given $30 in change,

2 Portable: People move from place to place. For this reason, it is important that money can be easily taken from place to place.

3 Durable: Australian money [notes] is made from polymer [plastic]. Prior to 1792, when the first polymer note was released,
notes were made of paper but they only lasted for approximately six months, As money changes hands frequently, it is important
that it lasts, or is durable,

& Scarce: Scarce means limited in amount. Given that money is in limited supply, it is of value to people, Money is in limited
supply because the Royat Australian Mint controls the money supply, The problem of inflation arises when too much money is
available. Inflation is an increase in the overall level of prices. With inflation a fixed amount of money buys fewer goods and
services than it did previously.

5 Acceptable: Money must be accepted by everyone. People must be confident that when they pay for a good or a service, their
money will be accepted as payment.

17 Case study: Choice ®}

As a consumer it is very difficult to compare every variety of product that is for sale. When deciding on a product it is very wise to
research the selection available, In light of the Latin phrase caveat emptor, let the buyer beware, consumers are responsible for
their purchases and therefore should choose carefully,

‘A magazine called Choice was established to provide consumers with information relating to product quality and performance.
Choice is an Australian magazine that is published in Marrickville, NSW, eleven times a year.

Choice reports on the testing of a variety of products. The people who work for Choice test a variety of the same product—for
example, a camera or a microwave—and present the information to the consumer. This enables the consumer to be aware of the
different models of products, their prices, standards and availability. Most importantly, it allows the consumer to get the best value
for their money for a particular product,

The staff at Choice purchase the products that they test from shops, as do normal consumers, because they want to act ethically.
When they comment on their findings they want to do so freely and without any commitment to another business that may have
given them the product free of charge, For example, if the staff at Choice find it difficult to obtain a particular product then they
will comment on this in the magazine.

Choice magazine includes various regular features, Examples include:

® ‘Choice Regulars (letters), which allows consumers to write to Choice magazine and voice their opinion on a certain product
‘® ‘Choice Reports’, which includes specialised reports on particular products
® ‘Choice Tests’, which presents information on a variety of products that have been tested by Choice employees

18 Foreign currency

Each country has its own currency which is legal tender within the borders of that country. Normally it cannot be used for cash
transactions in another country. Foreign currency refers to currency [money] of another country, other than the place in which the
person is located. For example, if you lived in Australia and you were to travel to Japan you would need to purchase Japanese yen,
In this example, Japanese yen is the foreign currency.

Being able to change one country’s money for another country’s money allows people to travel and trade [exchange goods and
services}. Exchanging one currency for another can usually be done in both countries, Imagine if you couldn't exchange money at
all. Going te anather country but not being able to purchase products [a drink, food and a night's accommodation] would make your
holiday a disaster! Fortunately, this is not the case.

The value of a country’s currency fluctuates according to its supply and demand on the world markets, Supply refers to the amount
of the currency that is available for sale. Demand refers to how sought after the currency is on the world markets. For example,
the value of the Australian dollar fluctuates on wortd markets according to the demand for it. In May 2000, the Australian dollar
was worth 58 US cents, but in June 2000, it was worth 54 US cents. Australian currency is measured against all currencies but due
to the strength of the USA's economy, the US dollar is used as a benchmark, A benchmark is a standard which all countries aim

to achieve.

19 Tax File Number

All three levels of Australian government—local, state and federal—collect taxes. Individuals and businesses make these
compulsory payments to the government. The governments use the money to provide infrastructure (schools, roads, hospitals etc.)
for people within the community. The Commonwealth government collects taxes from income lincome taxes].

The Australian Taxation Office [ATO] works on behalf of the government to process the collection of income tax. A tax return is a
declaration of income earned by a person or business, The ATO then calculates whether or not that person or business has paid
the correct amount of tax, The ATO may require the additional payment of tax or, alternatively, issue a tax refund, To make the
process of collection of taxes more efficient, the ATO introduced the tax file number [TFN] in 1989.

ATEN is a number issued by the ATO, It is issued to the following: an individual person, a company, a trust, a partnership or a
‘Superannuation fund.

Just as people and businesses have their own personal identification numbers for bank accounts, the ATO assigns a particular TFN
to each individual taxpayer who applies for one. The taxpayer keeps the allocated TFN throughout their life. Although it is not
compulsory to have a TFN, it is recommended that one be obtained,

People without a TFN may experience delays with the ATO processing financial information. Having a TFN allows 2 person's tax to
be calculated correctly, for without a TFN a person may pay more tax than is required.

Having a TFN assists people, as it is required in many circumstances, The following list highlights some of the circumstances in
which a person will need a TFN:

%& lodging a tax return Ideclaring their income and expecting a return of extra tax in the form of money)

% applying for certain income assistance or Support payments [such as Centrelink or benefits)

® paying Child Support Allowance

® starting or changing jobs {filling out an employment declaration form)

%® studying at a tertiary institution and wishing to defer payment under the Higher Education Contribution Scheme (HECS)

REMEMBER 
Civil law is concerned with disputes between individuals. The aim of civil cases is to 
obtain damages to compensate for loss suffered. The two main areas are:
• contract law, which concerns disputes that arise where a legally binding agreement 
has been breached by a party to the agreement
• tort law, which concerns disputes that arise where a wrongdoing causes personal 
injury, property damage and/or financial loss.

Case study: Franca
Franca was single and lived in a rental apartment with two friends. She had a casual office 
job and was studying part-time at university. She became friends with Alex, a young man 
who attended all the same lectures as her. Franca saw their relationship as platonic and 
believed Alex felt the same. One day he invited her over to his flat and Franca accepted.
Once there, however, she quickly regretted her decision. Alex made it clear he expected 
more, and became rough when Franca resisted. He told her he did not like women who 
played hard to get. Frightened and upset, Franca insisted she was not interested but he 
did not listen. Alex sexually assaulted Franca and her wrist was broken in the struggle.
Franca slid into a depression afterwards. Her broken wrist prevented her from working, 
and she was not entitled to sick leave. Her medical bills were costly and she was unable 
to pay her share of the rent. She dropped out of university because she could not bear to 
see Alex in the lectures. She felt her life was in a mess.
Franca was encouraged by her friends to make a report to the police. 
REMEMBER 
Legal wrongdoing is something that causes injury, damage or loss. Depending on 
the nature of the wrongdoing, it might be covered by criminal law or civil law. Some 
incidents can lead to action under both criminal and civil law.

Case study: Fred
Fred suspected his neighbours would still be asleep. It was six in the morning, and they 
had a late night last night. Fred had been kept awake until 4am by their loud party, and 
he was feeling jittery and irritable. He had tried talking to his neighbour George about the 
noise on past occasions, without success. Now was the time to take action.
George’s fat little dog barked most of the day; it had a high-pitched, hysterical bark that 
got on Fred’s nerves. He wondered how it would like a bucket of cold water poured over it. 
It didn’t like it much! Fred smiled. He was just warming up. He picked some rotten, maggot-
infested apricots off the grass and slung them over the fence. It was only fair, the tree 
belonged to George. He’d asked George to prune the branches overhanging the fence, but 
George had refused. Fred managed to get several into the pool. Then he reached over the 
fence and broke off a large branch. He dropped it, narrowly missing the dog.
Fred looked around the yard, wondering what else he could do. Before he could decide,  
he heard his front gate open and angry footsteps pounding down the side of his house. 
Fred stopped smiling.

6

REMEMBER 
Which court hears a civil case depends on the court’s jurisdiction and its position in  
the court hierarchy. Some types of cases are heard in federal courts, rather than  
state courts.
Case study: Insight Vacations v Young [2011] HCA 16 
This real-life case dealt with an injury that occurred to a tourist. Mrs Young bought a 
European holiday package from the tour company Insight Vacations. While on the coach, 
Young stood up and got out of her seat. The coach braked suddenly. Young fell and  
was injured.
Young sued Insight Vacations. She claimed the tour company did not exercise adequate 
care and skill. The case was heard in the District Court of New South Wales. Insight 
Vacations pointed to a clause in the contract that said they were not responsible for 
injuries if the passenger was not wearing a safety belt. Young won the case and was 
awarded damages (a sum of money).
Insight Vacations appealed. The case went up the hierarchy to the Supreme Court of  
New South Wales, Court of Appeal division. The damages were reduced, but Insight Vacations 
were still held to be responsible. The tour company then appealed to the High Court.
The High Court held that the clause in the contract was not valid because it tried to 
remove consumers’ rights, which are protected by law. The appeal failed.

Safety
Consumer protection laws also relate to the safety of goods and product-related services. 
The ACL created national safety standards, which include mandatory safety and information 
standards, and the removal from sale (recall) of unsafe goods.

12 Consumer credit
Renegotiating the terms of the loan
Some types of credit contract can be varied if the debtor is suffering from financial hardship. The 
debtor can approach the credit provider and ask to renegotiate the terms of the loan. The debtor 
can ask to extend the length of the loan and postpone repayment dates, or reduce the amount of 
each repayment. The loan still needs to be repaid, but it will be easier for the debtor to meet the 
repayments.
Under the National Consumer Credit Code, the credit provider must reply to the debtor’s request 
in writing within 21 days. If the provider does not agree to the request, they have to give reasons. 
They also need to name their External Dispute Resolution (EDR) scheme and explain the debtor’s 
rights under that scheme. All credit providers must belong to an EDR scheme.
1

2

unable to renegotiate their contract.
 
 
3

So far you have repaid $5000, in accordance with the repayment schedule. However, 
you recently lost your job and cannot afford your repayments. Write a letter to the bank 
manager, Ms Bigg, asking to renegotiate the terms of your loan. Suggest an alternative 
repayment schedule. Be persuasive!

Credit provided to Australian consumers is regulated by the National Consumer Credit 
Code. An individual who owes money is called a debtor.

Case study: Alexandra
Alexandra was in a relationship with Robert. She liked him very much but did not feel 
ready to settle down with anybody just yet. When they discovered she was pregnant, 
Robert proposed. Alexandra was not ready for marriage and did not think Robert was the 
right person for her. However, she was afraid she would not be able to support herself and 
her baby, so she agreed to the marriage.
13 Legal requirements of marriage
Family law
Consent to marry
The Marriage Act 1961 (Cth) outlines circumstances where consent to a marriage may not be 
considered real. These are:
• where consent was forced
• where consent was obtained by fraud
• the party was mistaken as to the identity of the person they were marrying
• the party was mistaken as to the nature of the wedding ceremony
• the party did not have the mental capacity to understand the nature and consequences of the  
wedding ceremony.
1

requirements for a marriage to be valid. List them.

states the conditions under which a marriage is void.
2

The law makes a distinction between employees and independent contractors. 
Employees are covered by workplace laws governing matters such as annual leave, sick 
pay and termination of employment; contractors are not.
Case study: Rania

takes work home with her. She is not permitted to write for other publications. Her editor 
assigns articles for her to write, but Rania decides how to write them and what material 
to include. Rania is paid a regular salary minus deductions for income taxation. Rania is

laws

2

3

4 
The Fair Work Act 2009 does not apply to contractors or to  
people employed in a particular job less than one year. 
 
 True

harsh, unjust or unexpected.

REMEMBER 
The unfair dismissal provisions under the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) apply to many 
Australian employees. Fair Work Australia, the national workplace relations tribunal, 
provides remedies for unfair dismissal.
Case study: Russell v Dyers Gippsland Transport  
[2009] FWA 887 
This real-life case involved an application for a remedy under the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). 
Mr Russell, an employee, claimed his dismissal from his job was unfair because it was 
harsh, unjust or unreasonable.
Russell was a truck driver, and his job involved driving groceries to supermarkets. He  
held the job for about one-and-a-half years. On the day he was dismissed, he had been 
driving through very bad weather. Mr Rendall, who also worked for the company, noticed 
that the truck had been damaged and that Russell had not reported it, which he was 
obliged to do. Russell stated the damage was caused by a tree. He said he was about to 
report the damage, but Rendall did not believe him. The employer decided to terminate 
Russell’s employment immediately. Russell had previously received two written warnings.
ISBN 978 1 92571 052 6

© Stella Tarakson and Blake Education 2012
35
Interactive Instant Lessons • Legal studies • Civil laws and processes
Workplace laws 
16 Unfair dismissal
8 
Was Russell’s application for a remedy for unfair dismissal accepted or rejected by  
the tribunal?
 
9 
a How long had Russell been employed by the company at the time he was dismissed?
 
b Would his ability to seek a remedy be different if he had held the job for under one  
year? Explain.
 
 
10

was unfair.
 
 
 
11 
a  Which of the three matters listed in Question 10 had not been properly satisfied in  
this case?
 
b The tribunal noted that even if Russell had been given that opportunity, it would have 
made no difference. Do you agree with the tribunal’s approach? Give reasons for  
your answer.
 
 
 
 
 
Russell claimed his termination was unfair because it was not his fault the damage 
occurred, as the employer sent him down residential streets with trees. He also claimed 
he was not given the opportunity to respond to the problem before he was dismissed. The 
employer noted that Russell’s damage record was several times higher than anyone else, 
suggesting he had problems performing the job properly. The employer also stated that all 
Russell had to do was report the damage – he was not personally responsible for fixing it. 
The tribunal agreed with the company, noting Russell’s high damage rate and prior warnings. 
It noted that although he should have been given a chance to respond on that day, it would 
not have altered the outcome even if he had a greater chance to defend himself.

17 Discrimination in the workplace
Discrimination complaints
If a person has been unlawfully discriminated against in the workplace, there are various 
avenues they can take, as shown in the diagram below. Anti-discrimination and/or rights bodies 
can investigate the complaint. Both sides will be listened to. Conciliation, which involves 
discussing the problem with a view to the parties reaching their own solution, may be attempted. 
Generally, it is only if these methods fail that a party will approach a court, as such action is 
stressful, time-consuming and expensive.
1 
Discrimination in the workplace on any ground or matter  
is unlawful. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 True     
 False
2 
In Australia, anti-discrimination laws exist at the federal level only.        
 True     
 False
3 
A matter may not amount to unlawful discrimination if it is an  
inherent feature of the job.  
 
 
 
 
 
       
 True     
 False
4 
Advertising for a person of a specific ethnic background to work in  
an ethnic-specific food restaurant is unlawful. 
 
 
 
       
 True     
 False
5 
Indirect discrimination is not unlawful because the action appears  
to apply to everyone equally. 
 
 
 
 
 
       
 True     
 False
6 
Requiring all employees to be fluent in English when this is not  
necessary for the job is an example of indirect discrimination. 
       
 True     
 False
REMEMBER 
Federal and state laws throughout Australia prohibit discrimination in the workplace. 
Discrimination can be either direct or indirect.

Shelter 
and tenancy

1 
The following rights and duties belong to landlords and tenants. Write them in the correct 
columns in the table.
a Keep the premises reasonably clean
b Keep the premises in a reasonable state of repair
c Quiet enjoyment of the property
d Not damage the property
e Inspect the premises
f Give correct notice of rent increases
g Not make alterations without consent
h Be reimbursed for damage caused by occupants or their guests
i Be paid rent on time
j Have reasonable locks and security
k Give correct notice if wanting to sell the house
l Not use premises for illegal purposes
Tenant rights
Tenant duties
Landlord rights
Landlord duties
REMEMBER 
The rights and duties of a tenant and landlord are governed by the residential tenancy 
agreement.
Case study: Chloe
Chloe rented a small home in a quiet suburb. It was built in the 1950s and showed the 
odd signs of wear and tear. A few of the bathroom tiles were cracked, the carpet was worn 
and the paint was blistered and peeling in the bedrooms. Other than that, the house was 
in reasonable condition. Chloe lived there with her two young children.

One day a water pipe burst in the kitchen. Chloe and her children were out at the time. 
When they returned home they discovered the place was flooded. The carpets were 
saturated. Water was still flowing. Chloe immediately turned off the stop cock and then 
called the agent. She reported the damage and the agent agreed to send out a plumber. 
Chloe waited for two days but the plumber did not turn up. She had no water and could 
not flush the toilets. She had called the agent several times and he kept assuring her that 
the plumber would arrive. Finally, Chloe got sick of waiting. She called a plumber herself 
and had the pipe fixed. She paid the plumber with her own money.
2 
Identify whose responsibility is it to maintain the premises and keep them in a reasonable 
state of repair.
 
3 
a  In your opinion, does a burst water pipe require an emergency repair, or is it the sort of 
repair that can wait?
 
b Do you think being made to wait two days to repair the pipe is reasonable? Explain.
 
 
4 
Chloe tried to claim the plumber’s bill back from the landlord, but he refused to pay. 
Identify who is responsible. Give reasons for your answer.
 
 
 
5 
The landlord inspected the damage and decided to replace the carpets. He stated 
Chloe should pay for the new carpets, claiming it was her fault the old ones were ruined. 
Do you agree with the landlord? Give reasons for your answer.
 
 
 
6 
Chloe is sick of battling with the landlord and decides to leave. She gives the correct  
notice period and finds a new home. When she leaves the agent informs her that she will 
lose her bond.
a Identify the circumstances under which a tenant may lose a bond.
 
b Do you think Chloe is entitled to get her bond back? Explain.

19 Purchasing a home
1 
Conveyancing involves the transfer of title:
a from the vendor to the purchaser.
b from the purchaser to the vendor.
c from the seller to the real estate agent.
d from the vendor to the seller.
2 
A private sale is:
a a sale that is not advertised.
b a sale where there are no open house inspections.
c a sale made directly by the vendor without the use of a real estate agent.
d not an auction.
3 
A cooling-off period:
a gives the vendor a few days in which to change their mind.
b gives the purchaser a few days in which to change their mind.
c gives both parties a few days in which to change their minds.
d does not apply to the sale of land.
REMEMBER 
Homes are usually placed on the market by real estate agents, but they can be put on 
the market by the vendor (seller).
Case study: Corban v Levett [1996] NSWSC 509 
In this real-life case, Mr Corban owned a property in a suburb of Wollongong, New South 
Wales. He claimed he had entered into an agreement to sell the property to Mr and Mrs 
Levett, who said no such agreement existed. The Supreme Court of New South Wales agreed 
with the Levetts. Corban then appealed to the Supreme Court’s Court of Appeal division.
The facts of the case are these. Corban engaged a real estate agent to sell the property. 
The agent negotiated with the Levetts, who were interested in purchasing. They agreed 
on a price of $200 000. They also discussed work that needed to be done on the property 
by Corban before the sale. Corban did in fact later carry out this work. The Levetts gave 
the agent a $20 000 cheque for the deposit, ‘subject to contract’. This meant the money 
would only be released to the seller once contracts were signed and exchanged, which 
never happened.
Corban claimed they had an oral (unwritten) agreement to enter into a formal, written 
agreement for the sale of the property. Corban sought damages and specific performance 
(an order requiring the other party to perform the contract). 
ISBN 978 1 92571 052 6

© Stella Tarakson and Blake Education 2012
41
Interactive Instant Lessons • Legal studies • Civil laws and processes

19 Purchasing a home
The Court of Appeal did not agree with Corban. The judges stated that paying the deposit 
‘subject to contract’ meant the money was given in expectation of a future contract being 
entered. It did not in itself amount to a contract. The court noted that contracts for the 
sale of property are normally in writing because the process is complex and covers issues 
that cannot generally be covered in oral negotiations.
The appeal was dismissed.
4 
This real-life case gives an example of disputes that can arise concerning the sale of land. 
Outline Corban’s side of the story.
 
 
 
 
5 
a Explain how specific performance might be applied in this case.
 
 
 
b Explain how damages might be applied in this case.
 
 
 
6 
Outline the Levetts’ side of the story.
 
 
 
 
7 
Identify the court that heard the appeal.
 
8 
a Did Corban win his appeal?
 
b Outline the court’s reasoning for its decision.

20 Mock civil hearing
Now it is time to bring civil law to life by running a mock hearing. Read the following preparatory 
material and refamiliarise yourself with earlier material, especially Unit 6: Civil hearings and  
Unit 9: Torts. This is a negligence case. The purpose is to determine whether the plaintiff is 
entitled to damages and, if so, how much.
Roles
Judge
Presides over the court, decides matters of law and rules on the evidence. 
Played by:  
Judge’s associate
The judge’s assistant. Keeps lists of objections made by barristers, as well as the judge’s 
responses to the objections. 
Played by:  
Court officer 
Opens and closes court, maintains order. Calls witnesses and administers the oath or affirmation. 
For example, the witness might say ‘I swear by Almighty God that the evidence I give will be the 
truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth’. An affirmation is similar but without the religious 
reference, and can begin ‘I solemnly and sincerely declare and affirm that ...’.
Also passes any relevant documents from barristers to the judge’s associate.
Played by:  
Court reporter 
Records proceedings, reads back transcript if required.
Played by:  
Jurors
Decide matters of fact. Their use in civil hearings varies between states and they would often not 
be used in such cases. There should be 4–6 jurors for the mock hearing.
Played by (4-6 people):  
 
 
 
Barristers
Present their clients’ cases. Make opening addresses, question witnesses and argue relevant 
points of law.

Barrister for defendant played by:

Case summary
Mabel, a 78 year old, was walking down the street with her grandson John, aged 19. They 
were talking and looking at each other as they walked. The street was lined with very 
large trees. In some places, tree roots had lifted up sections of the footpath, making it 
uneven. The local council had commenced work to repair the footpath. In one place, the 
council had cut the path into sections, leaving two unstable pieces of concrete. Mabel 
caught her shoe in the gap and lost her balance. John was unable to catch her in time. 
Mabel fell heavily and fractured her hip, thigh and elbow. She is suing the local council for 
damages, including her medical bills, the cost of nursing home care, loss of enjoyment of 
life and pain and suffering. 
Damages claim
Assume Mabel is claiming the following sums. They are not necessarily realistic figures.
• Hospitalisation and doctors’ fees: $10 000
• Ongoing care expenses: $45 000
•  Nursing home accommodation bond: $200 000
• Pain and suffering: $300 000.
The council will be trying to reduce how much they pay if the plaintiff wins.

3 Australia’s system of government
John
The danger was not obvious to us. People can’t be expected to watch their feet all the 
time. It was a bright sunny day but we did not notice anything. The council created the 
danger and should have either put up warning signs or a protective barrier. Nan and I 
have often walked down that street, and we did not expect to suddenly encounter such a 
problem.
Witness statements
Mabel
I was fairly active until that day. I lived alone and was able to look after myself. Now I am 
in respite care in a nursing home, and I have been told I have to stay permanently.  
I don’t like where I am staying, but I don’t want to move in with my children and become a 
burden. I am unable to care for myself and I am in constant pain. I take painkillers but they 
make me feel dizzy and nauseous. I have lost all enjoyment of life and I sometimes wish  
I could just die. My medical bills are very high and I am worried about the costs of nursing 
home accommodation. I might have to sell my home to get into a nursing home that I like.
Saunders, a local council representative
The council admits to having created the danger, but it was an obvious danger. Councils 
do not have a duty to warn of obvious dangers. Contributory negligence is an issue 
[meaning the plaintiff’s carelessness is partly or wholly to blame for the injury]. She was 
not looking where she was going and her shoes were slippery. She was at least partly to 
blame for her injury, if not entirely.
Alice (called as a witness for the defence)
I was walking behind Mabel and her grandson just before she fell. I noticed the gap in the 
footpath and was about to call out a warning. It was clear that they hadn’t seen it; I think 
they were too busy chatting. I was too late, however. I ran over when Mabel fell. I rang the 
ambulance while her grandson comforted her. I could tell the old lady was in extreme pain.

Courtroom tips
Tip 1: Court etiquette
Court etiquette requires that everybody stands when the judge enters or leaves the room. People 
entering or leaving the courtroom should bow to the judge’s bench as a mark of respect. Judges 
are referred to as ‘Your Honour’ and lawyers should stand while addressing the judge. Barristers 
should not argue with the judge. They can say ‘With respect, I submit that …’, but when a judge 
passes a ruling it must be accepted. An appropriate phrase is ‘If your Honour pleases’. Unlike in 
US courtroom dramas, Australian lawyers remain behind the bar table. They do not stride around 
or approach the witness stand. Lawyers refer to other lawyers as ‘my learned friend’. 
Tip 2: The art of cross-examination
The purpose of cross-examination is to challenge a witness’s evidence with a view to discrediting 
them. Although leading questions (questions that suggest their own answer) are not permitted 
in examination-in-chief, they are often used in cross-examinations. It is a rule among barristers 
never to ask a question in cross-examination that they do not know the answer to, as they might 
not get the answer they want. Once they have the information desired, they should stop asking 
questions and not give the witness the opportunity to continue talking. Demanding ‘yes’ or ‘no’ 
answers is acceptable, although the judge may allow the witness to explain themselves more fully.
Tip 3: Hostile witnesses
Barristers cannot ordinarily cross-examine their own witnesses. But if a witness gives evidence 
that favours the other side or contradicts evidence in their previous written statements, the 
barrister can try to have them declared hostile and is then able to cross-examine the witness.
Steps to take
  1 
Divide into small groups and allocate roles.
  2 
Arrange the room so that it looks like a courtroom.
  3 
Ensure everyone knows their role or character story.
  4 
The barrister for the plaintiff opens their case, then calls their first witness.
  5 
The witness is questioned by the plaintiff’s barrister, then by the defendant’s barrister.
  6 
This is repeated for each of the plaintiff’s witnesses.
  7 
The barrister for the defence opens their case and calls their first witness.
  8 
Each witness is questioned by the defence barrister, then by the plaintiff’s barrister.
  9 
The judge sums up then reaches a conclusion with the help of the jury (if there is one).
10 
The judge makes their decision, passes an order and explains it to the class.
Dr Wong
I am Mabel’s GP. It is my opinion that Mabel will never be able to live independently again. 
She needs constant care and a nursing home is the best place for her. Her condition is 
such that she will suffer chronic pain for the rest of her life. I believe her lifespan will 
be much shorter than it would otherwise have been. Mabel is suffering from depression 
brought on by her accident and has expressed a wish to die.

1 What is a crime?
1 Summary offence: less serious, heard by magistrate; 
indictable offence: more serious, heard by judge and jury. 
2 Consider: To reflect severity of offence, to speed up 
proceedings for less severe offences, to be able to make 
comparable sentencing decisions. 3 Consider: The process 
is generally faster, the accused might think a jury would 
not favour him or her, in hope of a less severe penalty. 
4 Evidence for serious indictable offences is received, 
examined and tested before a magistrate. If the magistrate 
decides there is enough evidence to warrant a trial, the 
case will go to a higher court before a judge and jury. 
If not, the accused is discharged. This saves time and 
expense. 5 The case is dismissed and the defendant is free 
to go. 6 a Regina, Latin for the Queen b The prosecution 
‘R’ is listed first because they commenced the proceedings. 
7 presumption; guilty; alleged; prove; burden; insanity; 
standard; high; reasonable; acquitted; convicted. 8 a theft 
b fraud c speeding d murder e trafficking f assault  
g abuse h vandalism.
2 The mental element
1 present: murder; absent: involuntary manslaughter; 
mitigated: voluntary manslaughter.  
2 a This was an honest mistake. To have stolen it, Ali 
would have had to have known it wasn’t hers and 
intended to deprive the rightful owner of it.  
b Perjury involves knowingly telling lies while giving 
evidence under oath. c Nathan was committing perjury. 
His motivation to lie does not matter. d Most likely  
this would be considered an unavoidable accident.  
e No, because Simon was not being reckless. He had no 
intention to hurt the old lady and did not even know she 
was there until she stepped out in front of the car.  
He was driving carefully and gave assistance. f Bribery  
is the offer of a payment with the intention of inducing 
the recipient to act contrary to their duty. g Ricardo 
dropped the money accidentally. He was not attempting 
to bribe the officer. h Fraud involves intentionally  
inducing someone to believe something that the person 
knows to be untrue, with the goal of financial gain.  
i Will committed fraud against his employer by putting  
in claims to be reimbursed for meals that he knew  
he did not have.
3 The physical element
1 c 2 b 3 a 4 c 5 c 6 An act is physical activity while an 
omission is the failure to do something that there was a 
duty to do. 7 a Miller had a duty because he created the 
dangerous situation in the first place. b Miller’s duty was 
to call the fire brigade. c Consider: Miller’s ability to put 
the fire out, the danger he would be exposed to, whether 
there should be a need to reduce the danger resulting 
from one’s actions. 8 a The decision was voluntary.  
b Even if Miller were still drunk at the time, it would most 
likely be voluntary. It might be involuntary if he did not 
become intoxicated voluntarily. Alternatively, it might be 
involuntary if he had slept through the night and was 
unaware of the fire.
4 Causation 
1 a The outcome would not have happened but for the 
defendant’s act or omission b The act or omission is an 
‘operative and substantial cause’ of the outcome c The 
sequence of events leading to the outcome. 2 a Would the 
victim have died but for the stabbing? No. It is likely to pass 
this test. b The stabbing was an operative and substantial 
cause. It did not need to be the only cause. The woman’s 
refusal was not enough in itself to be the main cause of 
death. It is likely to pass this test. c Blaue could not use the 
victim’s religious principles to avoid liability. d Would the 
victim had drowned but for being placed unconscious near 
the water. Not likely. It is not likely to pass this test. e The 
tide coming in is an ordinary act of nature. It did not break 
the chain of causation. The chain would only be broken 
if the victim had regained consciousness and voluntarily 
walked into the sea. f Extraordinary acts of nature that 
could break the chain could include an earthquake or a 
tsunami. A fire could also be an extraordinary event (but 
not if Hallet lit the fire). 3 The operation of the test itself 
is fair, because it would be unfair if the accused could 
escape liability by saying death was due to other causes, 
such as refusal to have a blood transfusion or the ordinary 
action of the sea. But there are some situations where the 
intervening act should result in a not guilty verdict, e.g. an 
extraordinary act as described in R v Hallet.

Case study: R v Miller [1983] 2 AC 161
Miller, who was homeless, had been out drinking and then returned to a house where 
he had been staying. He fell asleep with a lit cigarette in his hand. The cigarette started 
a small fire. Rather than putting it out, Miller went into another room and went back to 
sleep. The fire ended up causing extensive damage to the property. Miller was convicted 
of arson. The court ruled that the actus reus was not the starting of the fire, but Miller’s

the fire brigade.

REMEMBER 
People applying for legal aid may need to pass various tests. A means test might apply, 
which considers the applicant’s income and assets. A merit test might also be necessary.
Case study: Potier v Legal Aid Commission of  
New South Wales [2011] NSWSC 1066
The plaintiff, Mr Potier, claimed the Legal Aid Commission (LAC) was unreasonably slow 
and not acting in good faith regarding his legal aid applications. He wanted all of his 
applications to be funded without delay.
Mr Potier was in jail at the time. The crime was soliciting (arranging and paying for) the 
murder of his former partner and her boyfriend. Because of his prison sentence, Potier 
had to apply for court permission to commence proceedings against the LAC.
Under the relevant statute, the court had to be satisfied that:
• the proceedings were not an abuse of process (taking improper advantage of the system)
• there was a prima facie ground for the proceedings (prima facie is Latin for ‘at first face’ and 
means ‘on first sight or initial observation’).
The Supreme Court of New South Wales said the prima facie requirement meant that 
Potier had to have an arguable case that was not totally hopeless. It looked at his legal 
aid applications, which had been rejected under the merits test and were currently being 
reviewed. The court did not agree the LAC was acting in bad faith. The court also noted 
that the LAC ‘is charged with the important responsibility of allocating necessarily limited 
resources in accordance with its statutory duties and priorities’.  
The Supreme Court held that Potier had not demonstrated a prima facie case. It was 
therefore not necessary to consider the other requirement (abuse of process) because 
both would need to be proven for the case to succeed. Leave to commence proceedings 
was refused.

11 How do you plead?
The 
court 
system
1 
List three possible aggravating factors for a crime.
 
 
 
2 
List three possible mitigating factors for a crime.
 
 
 
3 
Explain why pleading guilty might reduce the sentence.
 
 
 
4

REMEMBER 
If the defendant pleads not guilty, a committal or trial will be set for a later date. If a 
defendant pleads guilty, there is no trial. When deciding a sentence, the court will look 
at the defendant’s personal situation and any aggravating or mitigating circumstances.
Case study: Assault in the night
Shortly after midnight, Mrs Olsen heard a pounding on the door. The 82 year old, who 
lived alone, was frightened and did not answer. The sound of smashing glass, however, 
brought her out of her bedroom. She saw two young men climb in through a window.  
The taller one demanded money. When Mrs Olsen refused, he pressed a knife to her  
throat. The smaller man found her handbag and removed $30 in notes and coins. She said 
that was all she had. Angered, the tall man punched her in the face and pushed her 
over. The two men ran outside, but were caught by police who had been alerted by a 
neighbour who had heard the window being smashed.
Ricky, the smaller man, was filled with remorse. He had only gone along with the idea 
because his friend Sam had insisted. Ricky was going through a bad patch. He had lost 
his job and his girlfriend had left him. He was behind on rent and his landlord was 
threatening eviction. This was the first time he had broken the law. 
Sam, however, had three previous convictions for breaking and entering. In each case the 
victim was an elderly woman living alone. Sam deliberately targeted Mrs Olsen because 
she was vulnerable. He felt no pity for the old lady, who broke her hip when she fell and 
required hospitalisation. All he felt was anger at being caught.

REMEMBER 
Evidence refers to things that establish a crime was committed, and may form a 
link between the crime and the criminal. Three types of evidence are real evidence, 
documentary evidence and oral evidence.
Case study: Looking for evidence
Erin was reported missing by her flatmate. Two days later, the police found Erin’s body 
hidden in isolated bushland. The autopsy found she had died from knife wounds. There 
had been no witnesses to the murder, but a neighbour heard Erin arguing with her 
boyfriend on the night she went missing. Her boyfriend, Harry, was questioned by the 
police. They found that bike tracks and footprints at the crime scene matched his bike  
and shoes. Soil on his tyres and shoes was of the same type as that at the crime scene.  
No fingerprints or bloodstains were found on the knife in the creek, which had been 
washed clean by the running water.

14 Trial procedures
Examining a witness
Examining a witness is a skill. It is important for the lawyer to listen to the answers and respond 
accordingly, rather than simply reading out a list of prepared questions. 
The aim of an examination-in-chief is to have the witness tell the story in their own words. 
Lawyers are not meant to ask leading questions of their own witnesses. A leading question is one 
that suggests its own answer. It directs the answer given by the witness and may sound more like 
a statement than a question. It could result in a ‘yes’ or ‘no’ answer rather than an explanation.
Leading questions are permitted in cross-examination, however. The purpose of a cross-
examination is to reveal the truth. Lawyers might try to show that a witness is lying, has a bad 
memory, or was unobservant or biased. The opposing side tries to cast doubt on the witness’s 
testimony; the other side might be able to clear this up in their re-examination. 
2 
The following questions are made in an examination-in-chief and they are leading 
questions. Rephrase them so that the opposing side will not be able to object.
a Did you see Francis enter the bedroom?
 
b You were at your office at 5pm, weren’t you?
 
c The traffic lights turned green as you approached, didn’t they?
 
Leading questions are allowed on some preliminary matters during examination-in-chief; for example, 
‘You are Mabel Smith, aged 44 years, and working as a receptionist in the defendant’s clinic?’
3

permitted in cross-examination.

15 The purposes of punishment
1 
Identify the court that heard this case.
 
2 
Outline the purpose of Fleming’s application.
 
 
REMEMBER 
When people break criminal laws, they are punished. Most punishments reflect elements 
of deterrance, rehabilitation, incapacitation or retribution.
Case study: R v Fleming [2006] QCA 26 
R v Fleming involved an application to appeal against the severity of a sentence. The 
Queensland Supreme Court, Court of Appeal division, commented on the purposes of 
criminal punishment in this case. 
Fleming, a 45-year-old unemployed man, wanted to appeal against his prison sentence.  
He had threatened to injure two public officers who were conducting an approved 
inspection on his property. The purpose of the visit was to inspect for the presence of 
unregistered dogs, and Fleming tried to stop them carrying out their duties. He was 
abusive, made obscene gestures and threatened violence.
Fleming had a long history of abusive and violent criminal offending, dating back to when 
he was a teenager. He had never been imprisoned, but always fined or given community 
service orders (orders to perform work to benefit the community). He regularly breached 
these orders.
This time, Fleming was imprisoned for four months, but allowed out early on condition 
he broke no further laws. The maximum penalty the judge could have given him for this 
offence was five years’ imprisonment. Fleming claimed he should not have been given 
a prison sentence. He noted he had pleaded guilty early on, and was suffering from 
depression. 
The Court of Appeal said the judge who passed the sentence was entitled to order 
imprisonment because:
• there was a need to protect public officers carrying out their lawful duties
• the applicant had a record of persistently offending.
The court noted: ‘The sentencing judge was perfectly entitled to identify this as a 
reasonable opportunity to impose a penalty which might at last work some actual 
personal deterrence.’
The application for leave to appeal was refused.

18 Young offenders
Special 
situations
REMEMBER 
In Australia, the statutory minimum age of criminal responsibility is 10 years old. There 
is a legal presumption that a child between the ages of 10 and 14 is not capable of 
committing a criminal act. Young people over 14 but not yet 18 are considered fully 
responsible for any offence they might commit, but they are not treated the same  
as adults.
1 
a  Do you think it is a good idea for a young offender and their family to meet with the 
victim, in a safe and controlled environment? Explain the reasons for your answer.
 
 
b Are there any situations where you think this would not be suitable? Explain the reasons 
for your answer.
 
 
2 
In your opinion, is it fair that the names of young offenders in the Children’s Court cannot 
be published? Explain the reasons for your answer.
 
 
Case study: Kelly and Tara
Kelly, aged 9, and her sister Tara, aged 11, went to their local shopping mall. They wanted 
to buy some costume jewellery with their pocket money. They entered a store and made 
their selection, then realised they didn’t have enough cash. Tara replaced a set of cheap 
bangles on the stand, but Kelly picked them up and slipped them into her pocket. Tara 
hesitated a moment before taking an extra set for herself and hiding them in her bag. 
Neither girl had broken the law before. They paid the shop assistant for all the goods 
except the bangles. As they tried to leave the store the assistant accused them of 
shoplifting and called the police.
3 
Can Kelly be charged by the police? Explain the reasons for your answer.
 
 
4 
a Can Tara be charged by the police? Explain the reasons for your answer.

b Explain what the police would have to try to prove in a case against Tara.
 
 
5 
Given this was a first offence and the value of the stolen items was very low, what course  
of action would the police most likely take?
 
 
6 
Explain how your answer would differ if the girls had shoplifted before, and the value of  
the items was high.
 
 
Case study: Joshua
Joshua’s parents went away for the weekend, leaving him alone in the house. Joshua, 
aged 16, decided to invite some friends over. He invited five of his mates from school and 
they planned to order pizza and watch the Friday night footy. Joshua packed some beer 
cans in the fridge in preparation. His friends arrived, but then a large group of teenagers 
Joshua barely knew gatecrashed. He tried to hold them off but failed. Some brought 
bottles of whisky; some brought joints. They were rowdy and played music very loudly. 
The police arrived in response to a noise complaint. Joshua had a joint in his pocket that 
he had accepted from an insistent girl, but he had no intention of smoking it. He was 
searched by the police.
7 
Was Joshua old enough to be charged by the police without them having to show he  
thought he was acting wrongfully? Explain the reasons for your answer.
 
 
8 
When Joshua packed beer in the fridge for himself and his friends, was he breaking  
the law? Explain the reasons for your answer.
 
 
9 
Was Joshua breaking the law by possessing cannabis, even though he had no intention  
of smoking it? Explain the reasons for your answer.
 
 
10 
Assume the police believed Joshua about the gatecrashers and the cannabis. Describe  
the action the police would most likely take.

1 
Read the following information then answer the questions below using the material  
in this text plus the Internet. 
REMEMBER 
International crimes include transnational crimes (which affect more than one 
nation), crimes that occur in international waters or airspace, and crimes that are so 
reprehensible they are seen as being against the whole of the international community.
Case study: Gaddafi
The year 2011 saw the end of the 42-year Gaddafi regime in Libya. Gaddafi’s early actions 
included shutting down American and British military bases, expelling Italian settlers and 
banning the non-Arab Berber language from schools. The regime became increasingly 
fundamentalist Islamic and sponsored anti-Western terrorist attacks. Dissent within the 
country was brutally stamped out. People trying to form a political party were executed, 
and it was illegal to talk to foreigners about politics. Gaddafi threatened to kill dissidents 
who escaped the country.
Political protests grew and intensified in 2011, sparking off a civil war between Gaddafi 
loyalists and rebel forces. Demonstrators and unarmed civilians were massacred. In June 
2011, the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued a warrant for Gaddafi’s arrest for crimes 
against humanity; however, Libya refused to acknowledge the authority of the ICC. 
The end of the regime came on 20 October 2011. Gaddafi was captured and killed by 
rebel Libyan forces. Some reports stated he was killed in crossfire; others claimed he was 
deliberately executed.
a 
Visit the website of the ICC at http://www.icc-cpi.int. In your own words, outline the  
role of the ICC.

20 Mock criminal trial
Now it is time to bring the criminal law to life by running a mock trial. Read the following 
preparatory material and refamiliarise yourself with earlier material, especially Unit 13: Rules of 
evidence and Unit 14: Trial procedures. The classroom can be set up to mimic a courtroom (see 
Unit 9: Criminal courts).
The use of time limits during the trial will ensure everyone has a fair opportunity. The opening 
addresses are limited to 5 minutes each, examination and cross-examination to 15 minutes each, 
re-examination to 5 minutes and closing addresses to 10 minutes each.
Roles
Judge
Presides over the court, decides matters of law and rules on the evidence. The judge should be 
played by the teacher, who ideally should keep notes of the proceedings.
Judge’s associate
The judge’s assistant. Keeps track of time and ensures time limits for mock trial are kept. Keeps 
lists of objections made by barristers, as well as the judge’s responses to the objections. 
Played by:  
Court officer 
Opens and closes court, maintains order. Calls witnesses and administers the oath or affirmation. 
For example, the witness might say ‘I swear by Almighty God that the evidence I give will be the 
truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth’. An affirmation is similar but without the religious 
reference and can begin ‘I solemnly and sincerely declare and affirm that . . .’. 
Also passes any relevant documents from barristers to the judge’s associate.
Played by:  
Court reporter 
Records proceedings, reads back transcript if required. This role can be omitted if there are not 
enough students; however, it is still a good idea to make a video or audio recording.
Played by:  
Corrective services officer
Guards the accused in the courtroom and escorts them in and out of the courtroom. Role can be 
omitted if there are not enough students.
Played by:  
Jurors
Decide matters of fact and determine whether accused is guilty or not guilty. The mock trial 
should have 12 jurors if possible, but can have less if there are not enough students.
Played by:

Prosecuting barrister
Presents the case for the prosecution. Makes an opening address, questions witnesses and 
argues relevant points of law. If the class is large, it can have a team of two or more barristers 
who do the preparation together but question different witnesses.
Played by:  
Barrister for the defence
Presents the case for the defence. Otherwise, the role is the same as for the prosecuting 
barrister.
Played by:  
Solicitors
Assist the barristers in preparing their cases. Sit near barristers at bar table and take notes of 
the proceedings. May help barristers by pointing out relevant matters during the trial. Can be 
omitted if not enough students, otherwise there should be one or two per side.
Played by:

Jason has pleaded not guilty to the charge of murder. He claims to have no knowledge of how 
the victim died.
Jason played by:

Should study the witness statements produced in these pages and answer questions accordingly, 
as far as possible. If necessary, witnesses can make up supporting details but should try not to 
contradict the given material. Expert witnesses can give their opinions, unlike other witnesses.

Case summary
Yvonne and Cara have been friends for many years. They grew up together in a rural town 
and had recently started sharing a flat in the city where they were attending university. 
On the night of the murder the girls caught a bus to town. They went to a nightclub 
where they met two young men, Jason and Nikolas. They got along well, and Jason bought 
drinks for the girls. At 10pm Yvonne said she was feeling nauseous and dizzy and wanted 
to go home. She refused any help and said she’d catch the bus. Cara got back to the flat 
at 2am. She checked on Yvonne and thought she was asleep. The next morning, however, 
she realised that Yvonne was dead.
