Bus driver
The victim boarded my bus around 10pm. She was swaying and looked very sleepy.  
I thought she’d been drinking and I remember hoping she didn’t throw up on my bus.  
She stumbled on her way out, as if she had trouble seeing. I often have drunks on my bus, 
but I thought it was a bit early in the night for someone to get that sloshed.
Witness statements
Remember, witnesses can be mistaken. They might not have seen what they thought they saw, 
or their memory may be flawed. Or they might lie – to cover up for others or to hide a secret, 
innocent or otherwise.
Cara
I only wished I’d gone home with Yvonne when she said she felt sick. But I liked Nikolas  
and wanted to stay. Jason left around 10 minutes after Yvonne. I thought he wanted  
to leave me and Nikolas alone. I feel awful thinking how I was out having fun when my  
friend needed me. Nikolas and I left the nightclub at 1.30am. He caught my bus with me 
and walked me to the flat. He left me at the door and caught another bus home. I looked 
in on Yvonne. I asked her if she was ok. She didn’t answer and I didn’t want to wake her. 
The next morning she was late getting up. I went in her room and checked. She was very 
pale and her skin felt cold. She wasn’t breathing, so I called the ambulance. 
Bartender
I recognise the defendant. He is a regular at the nightclub. Each time I see him he is with 
a different girl. He doesn’t talk to me much so I don’t know much about him. He kept 
ordering his usual drinks – scotch and cola. I noticed the victim leaving rather early. She 
walked right past me, and I remember thinking the defendant must have bombed out 
that time. The victim looked unsteady on her feet. I thought she was drunk. I didn’t notice 
when the defendant left. It was a busy night.
Nikolas
Jason and I are good mates and have known each other for years. Jason’s always picking 
up girls. I’m a bit shy, but he’s really out there. Most nights we go out he scores. I thought 
he was going to score with Yvonne but she got up and left early. Jason offered to take her 
home but she refused. Not long after she left he got up. He winked at me and walked out. 
I think that meant for me to carry on. Jason might be a bit of a flirt but he’s harmless.  
He’s a good bloke and would never hurt anyone.

20 Mock criminal trial
Jason
Yvonne was not my type. I only went along with things as I could see Nikolas fancied the other one. 
Yvonne was quiet and grumpy. I bought her a few drinks but she didn’t lighten up. She got drunk 
easily, too. When she left I didn’t care. I went a bit later, thinking I should leave Nikolas to it. I wasn’t 
fussed – win some, lose some. After I left I went straight home. I live on my own. I watched TV for a 
few hours then went to bed.
Forensic evidence
Yvonne’s autopsy found she had died of suffocation. The findings were consistent with someone 
holding a pillow over her face. There were no signs of struggle. This was explained by high 
levels of Rohypnol found in her blood. Rohypnol is a prescription drug for insomnia that is also 
known as a ‘date rape’ drug. Its symptoms include nausea, dizziness, problems seeing and talking, 
sleepiness and passing out. There is no evidence as to who put the drug in Yvonne’s drink. The 
autopsy found she did not have sexual intercourse that night. [Hint: Whoever plays the pathologist 
should do some further research into the effects of Rohypnol, and perhaps suffocation.]
Courtroom tips
Tip 1: Court etiquette
Court etiquette requires that everybody stands when the judge enters or leaves the room. People 
entering or leaving the courtroom should bow to the judge’s bench as a mark of respect. Judges 
are referred to as ‘Your Honour’ and lawyers should stand while addressing the judge. Barristers 
should not argue with the judge. They can say ‘With respect, I submit that . . . etc.’, but when a 
judge passes a ruling it must be accepted. An appropriate phrase in those circumstances is ‘If 
your Honour pleases’. Unlike in American courtroom dramas, Australian lawyers remain behind 
the bar table. They do not stride around or approach the witness stand. Lawyers refer to other 
lawyers in court as ‘my learned friend’. 
Tip 2: The art of cross-examination
The purpose of cross-examination is to challenge a witness’s evidence with a view to discrediting 
them. Although leading questions are not permitted in examination-in-chief, they are often used in 
cross-examination. It is a rule among barristers never to ask a question in cross-examination that 
they do not know the answer to, as they might not get the answer they want. Once they have the 
information desired, they should stop asking questions and not give the witness the opportunity to 
continue talking. Demanding ‘yes’ or ‘no’ answers is acceptable, although the judge may allow the 
witness to explain themselves more fully.
Tip 3: Hostile witnesses
Barristers cannot ordinarily cross-examine their own witnesses. However, if a witness gives 
evidence that favours the other side or contradicts evidence they had given in previous written 
statements, the barrister can try to have the witness declared hostile. The barrister is then able 
to cross-examine the witness.
Tip 4: Have fun!
Few things match the drama of the criminal courtroom. Part of a barrister’s skill is to present 
their case in an engaging and entertaining manner, which helps get the jury on side. The best 
way to do this is to enjoy yourself and add a touch of theatre!

Your task is to follow these directions on the given map to reach a final 
destination. This journey introduces you to some of the features of maps 
and calculations involving scale, distance, speed and time.
Keep track of each distance you cover, and your speed for each distance 
- at the end, you’ll be asked to calculate your total distance, total driving 
time and average speed. 
Map scale
1 
Look at the scale on your map.  
It is a graphic scale and looks like a long rectangle divided into black and white 
sections of equal size.  
 
Each small rectangle indicates a length on your map.  
The measurements above the scale indicate the matching length in real life. 
a Measure the divisions and reproduce them below. 
 
b Now label the scale above with the distances in real life indicated by each division. 
Include the units.   
2 
Use the scale you reproduced above to answer the following questions. 
a What distance in real life does the length of  
one rectangle on your scale represent?
b What distance in real life does the length of  
four rectangles on your scale represent?
c What length on your map indicates 1 km in real life?
d What distance in real life does 2 cm on your map represent?
3 
Complete the rule below.
 
Distance in real life in metres ÷             = length in centimetres on the map.
Grid references
These street maps use grid references to help you locate features such as particular streets or 
railway stations. For example, Preston railway station has the grid reference F11. This means 
that it is located in column F, row 11. 
When you find it on your map, you will see that some of the station icon is in row 12. 
However, most of it is in row 11, so this is the grid reference given.

Antarctica is situated in the  Arctic / Antarctic  Circle, and is surrounded by the  Northern / Southern  Ocean. 
It is the southernmost  country / continent , and is the  location / place  of the South Pole. The Antarctic stretches 
over 14 million square  kilometres / metres . About 98% of the land mass is covered by  ice / icicles . The average  
thickness / size  of the ice is 1.6 kilometres. Antarctica is the  warmest / coldest  continent and is very windy. 
It experiences very  little / small  precipitation as rain, so is technically classified as a desert. Plants that have  
alternated / adapted  to the cold can survive there, with the main flora being species of moss, lichen and algae. 
The region is  population / populated  by penguins and other sea birds, seals, whales and fish. Few other creatures 
can survive the  frozen / freezing  temperatures.

Understanding latitude
Lines of latitude
1 Complete the passage below using words from the box.
Imagine we could cut the Earth exactly in half along the theoretical line we call the E — — — — — —. The flat, 
cut surface is what we call the Equatorial plane. The middle of that plane is the Earth’s core and its angle is 
z — — — degrees because it is the absolute c — — — — — of the planet. To pinpoint a location on the Earth’s 
surface, we imagine drawing a l — — — between zero and the point being described. This line creates an 
a — — — — of elevation above the Equator, or below it. These are what we call angles of latitude.
Because the Equator is a circle of 360 d — — — — — —, angles of latitude are measured in degrees of arc, minutes 
of arc and seconds of arc. These minutes and seconds are not the same as ordinary t — — — measurements. They 
relate to the time it takes the Earth to r — — — — —. The maximum latitude angle possible is 90 degrees north or 
south from the imaginary zero point at the Earth’s core. There are two such locations: the N — — — —  Pole and 
the South Pole.

Understanding longitude
Lines of longitude
1 Complete the passage below using words from the box.
longitude               half               London               single               imaginary               curved 
meridian                 reference                 west                 measured                 circumference                 coordinates
Angles of longitude are determined by the use of i— — — — — — — — lines (or meridians) running from the North 
Pole to the South Pole. They start at a single point (the North Pole), bulge out around the Earth’s c— — — — — 
surface, then return to reach a s— — — — — point at the South Pole. A longitude number shows the point where a 
certain m — — — — — — — meets the Equator. Every meridian crosses the Equator, so the Equator is the point of 
r— — — — — — — — for all longitude measurements. Zero degrees north / south and 90 degrees east / west 
are the c— — — — — — — — — — of the North and South Poles. These lines of longitude are m — — — — — — — 
from the central line, which is located at Greenwich in L — — — — —, England. The global standard of time 
measurement also has Greenwich as its base reference. The Greenwich Meridian is considered to represent zero  
degrees l— — — — — — — —. These angles are measured from zero to 180 degrees east or w— — — of the 
Greenwich Meridian. The location 180 degrees east of the Greenwich Meridian is the same as the location 180 degrees 
west, because 180 degrees is h— — — of the Equator’s total c— — — — — — — — — — — — (360 degrees).

HINT:  Lines of longitude look like the segments of a 
peeled orange, starting at a Pole at a single point 
then curving out over the Earth’s surface and 
meeting at a single point at the opposite Pole.
At the 180 degree line of longitude in the Pacific Ocean is a 
theoretical line, known as the International Date Line, that 
separates the two hemispheres. In order to accommodate the 
locations of various island countries, this imaginary line is not 
perfectly straight. Travelling east across the line requires you to 
subtract 24 hours from today’s date. To the left of the line, the 
date is always one full day ahead of the date for the locations 
to the right.
GMT (Greenwich Mean Time) is now known 
as Coordinated Universal Time (abbreviated 
to UTC). Sometimes, it is written as GMT/
UTC. UTC is the standard time zone from 
which we measure all the other time zones 
across the world.

Creatures of the Antarctic
5  Read the information below and write definitions for the terms in bold, using your existing knowledge and the 
context to infer meaning.
Colossal squid have an average length of 12–14 metres, making them the world’s biggest invertebrates. They have the 
largest eyes of any species in the animal kingdom. They hunt prey using bioluminescence – emitting light to dazzle and 
confuse the intended victim. Two of their common targets are the Patagonian toothfish and the Antarctic toothfish.
Patagonian toothfish are predatory fish, closely related to Antarctic toothfish. They are found in the cold waters of many 
oceans, including the Southern Ocean of the Antarctic region. Their average weight is 9 to 10 kilograms and some are as 
long as 2.3 metres. They have extraordinary longevity; some toothfish have been known to live for up to 50 years. They 
feed on squid, smaller fish and prawns.
Sperm whales prey on various types of squid. Adult sperm whale bulls grow to around 15 metres long. Many sperm 
whales have scars on their backs, apparently caused by the barbed tentacles of the colossal squid.
Albatrosses are large seabirds that live in the Southern Ocean region. The Great Albatross has the largest wingspan of 
any bird species alive today, and can fly vast distances. Albatrosses are colonial birds who choose a mate for life, and 
nest in communities. They feed on squid, including the colossal squid, and fish and krill. Nineteen of the twenty-one 
species of albatross are currently considered to be endangered.

Topographic maps provide area references and grid references. An area reference is a four-digit number listing the 
eastings and northings, which tell us the square in which to find a feature. A grid reference is a six-digit number that 
gives us the exact point of a feature in the grid. In grid references, the third and sixth numbers tell us the tenths 
between the whole numbers marked on the grid, to enable us to locate a precise point.

How to draw a pie chart
This pie chart shows the top 10 gold medal winning nations in the 2008  
Beijing Olympic Games. The data for each country is as follows: China (51),  
USA (36), Russia (23), Great Britain (19), Germany (16), Australia (14), South 
Korea (13), Japan (9), Italy (8), and France (7). This pie chart was created  
using the following steps.
1  Add the numbers to obtain a grand total of medals = 196.
2   The whole circle is 360 degrees. Divide this by the grand total to find 
out how many medals are represented by one degree of angle:  
306 ÷ 196 = 1.836734694.
3   Multiply each country’s medal tally by the factor 1.836734694 to obtain 
each angle, and round off to one decimal place: China = 93.7°, USA = 66.1°, 
Russia = 42.2°, Great Britain = 34.9°, Germany = 29.4°, Australia = 25.7°, 
South Korea = 23.9°, Japan = 16.5°, Italy = 14.7°, France = 12.9°.
4   To measure the angles in the circle, place a protractor along the 90° vertical 
radius, and measure the first angle. Repeat for each angle, each time 
measuring from the line last added.
5   Use a shading or colouring key to identify the segment that represents 
each nation.

Acronyms in geography
An acronym is an abbreviation formed from the first letter or letters of words. Strictly speaking, an acronym forms an 
abbreviation that can be pronounced as a word (e.g. UNICEF). Abbreviations pronounced as a series of single letters 
(e.g. HTML) are called initialisms.

Contemporary issues in geography

The spatial and ecological dimensions of geography
When geographers investigate a contemporary issue, they work within the spatial dimension and the ecological 
dimension. The spatial dimension seeks to deal with where things are located and why they are there. The ecological 
dimension deals with how organisms (including humans) interact with elements of the spatial dimension – what we 
call ‘environments’.

Why	do	some	people	go	into	business?	
Case	study:	Angelina	Drano
Angelina Drano left school and worked for 
a plumber for wages. She went to a TAFE 
college to do her apprenticeship and gained a 
plumbing certificate. She was a fully qualified 
plumber, and decided she would rather have a 
plumbing business of her own. She no longer 
wanted to work for someone else, she wanted 
to work for herself. 
She had saved up some money but this 
was not enough to begin a business, so she 
approached her bank to apply for a loan. 
With the money she now had she purchased 
a truck and some tools and equipment. She 
advertised in the local newspaper to let people 
know she was available to do plumbing jobs 
in the area. She found it was important to 
quote competitively for jobs. If she charged 
too much, nobody would hire her – but if she 
charged too little, she couldn't cover her costs.
As a one-person business, Angelina was 
responsible for all the tasks that running 
a business required. This included making 
phone calls, ordering supplies, quoting on jobs 
and keeping business records. 
She found that if the income she received 
from her customers was greater than her 
expenses, such as repayments on the loan, 
purchase of supplies and renewing tools and 
equipment, she had made a profit. This profit, 
she felt, was the reward for taking the risk 
of possibly losing money. However, if her 
expenses exceeded her income, this would 
amount to a loss. 
Fortunately for Angelina she was successful 
and made enough profit for her to continue 
her business. She figured that, if she later got 
into difficulties and her business ran at a loss, 
she could always go back and work for a boss, 
for wages.
Important	terms	
Business: an organisation which sells goods or 
services for a profit
Capital: the money initially invested in a 
business
Company: a form of business which exists 
separately from its owners
Enterprise: organisational skills needed to 
produce goods and services; also another name 
for a business
Entrepreneur: someone who owns and runs a 
business
Expenses: costs involved in the process of 
earning money
Income: money which comes into the business, 
usually from sales
Loss: when expenses exceed income
Partnership: a business that is owned by two or 
more people
Profit: the reward for risk-taking; the excess of 
income over expenses
Proprietor: the owner of a business
Sole trader: a business that has only one owner

wages.	I	don't	want	
to	take	risks.
I	want	to	work	for	
myself	and	earn	bucket	
loads	of	money!

What are the necessary qualities of a successful businessperson? Sometimes luck plays a part, but 
other factors are much more important. The checklist below is a useful guide to the qualities that a 
good businessperson should have.  
Qualities	checklist	–	the	top	ten
2	Qualities	of	a	good	businessperson
Matthew	and	Andrew	Italia	–	Terrafirma	Technologies
Even when he was at primary school Matthew Italia helped his teachers to fix computers and solve 
their IT problems. So it wasn’t a surprise when Matthew started up his own small IT business as a 
teenager. Later he went on to register and operate the business in busy, central Geelong as a 21-year-
old. Starting as a sole trader, Matthew later went into partnership with his younger brother, Andrew, 
who showed the same IT problem-solving capabilities. 
Their business, Terrafirma Technologies, provides IT-related services. They targeted the small business 
sector and home users.
“We source and provide software and hardware at competitive prices, and advise people so they can 
get the most out of their IT system. A lot of people with small home offices also use our services as 
they lack the backup of an IT specialist that a bigger company can offer,” Matthew said.
“We also rectify computer faults, update computer security systems, and I have provided advice in 
networking, Internet connections, telecommunications systems and mobile phone systems.”
Matthew has a degree in Internet computing from R.M.I.T. while Andrew is currently studying a 
Bachelor of Information Technology, majoring in computer security and fraud detection. 
“I had always fixed computers for friends and family, but the turning point for me came in Year 10, 
when I completed work experience at a local computer store,” Matthew said.
“I realised I could explain difficult concepts about technology in ways that people without much IT 
knowledge and experience could understand. The work experience gave me the confidence to take the 
step towards starting my own small business.”
Matthew likes working with his brother as he finds they complement each other’s skill sets. “It's great 
bouncing ideas off each other about how to improve our business, and know that we will be the ones 
who reap the benefits of working hard together.” 
“We respect each other’s knowledge and opinions, but feel comfortable to challenge each other as 
well,” Andrew said.
“Our families have always been in small business and we have an uncle who mentors us and provides 
us with advice and feedback.”
Most of their initial business was generated through word-of-mouth, but they still needed to expand 
their client base to support themselves in full-time jobs. They have found that advertising their 
business through well-known computer journals and in local newspapers has helped to attract new 
clients.
“It’s very demanding running your own business and you have to have a wide range of skills besides 
just knowing a lot about IT. You need accounting and marketing skills as well as knowing how to 
provide great customer service,” Andrew says.
“We aren’t sure what our next step in the business will be – whether to open retail premises or employ 
staff – there is always a lot of planning and ‘thinking ahead’ in small business, and that’s what we 
love.”
q leadership
q capacity for hard work
q ability to handle stress
q ability to make hard decisions
q competitive spirit
q ability to accept responsibility
q adaptability
q flexibility
q courtesy
q concern for others
The following case study illustrates the importance of these qualities for the success of a business.

Living and Work Literacy 3
Anyone wanting to go into business needs to be aware of the different types of business 
organisations and the laws which affect them. Most people going into a business for the first time 
will become a sole trader but may later decide to form a partnership. Setting up a company is 
more complex.
Business	organisations		
3	Business	organisations
Geeta Pivari owns her own business as a 
hairdresser.
Her business is small in size.
She is responsible for the success or 
failure of the business.
She has unlimited liability. (If the 
business fails, Geeta as the owner 
suffers the loss.)
Geeta’s type of business is the most 
common form of business in Australia.
Businesses like Geeta’s usually 
consist of corner stores, small farms, 
trades people (such as carpenters, 
electricians, plumbers, computer 
technicians).
Geeta Pivari is a sole trader.
•
•
•
•
•
Goodfellas is the name of a business selling 
computer software. It is a company and 
therefore exists separately from its owners.  
It has perpetual succession and is known as 
an entity (it continues despite the death or 
bankruptcy of any of its owners).
The owners of Goodfellas are the 
shareholders, who have put varying sums of 
money into the company.
The liability of these shareholders is limited, 
meaning that shareholders can only lose the 
value of their shares (or the money they put 
into the company).
The shareholders are entitled to a share 
of the profits of the company, normally in 
proportion to their shareholdings.
Last year the profit of Goodfellas was $200 
000. This was paid as dividends to the 
shareholders.
Goodfellas is managed by Jake Pegg who 
is the Chief Executive Officer (CEO). He is 
responsible to a Board of Directors (elected 
by the shareholders).
In future years, Goodfellas' Board of Directors 
may decide to put some of the profits back 
into the company to help it expand.
Goodfellas is a company.
•
•
•
•
•
•
•
Dario Salazer and Alan Monie own a business 
repairing motor vehicles.
They share the workload equally (but they 
don’t have to).
They share in the profits (again not necessarily 
in equal shares, depending on their 
agreement).
They have formalised their agreement 
in writing in the form of a partnership 
agreement, which sets out how the 
partnership is organised (in case of disputes).
As partners, they have unlimited liability. 
(If the partnership fails, Dean and Alan 
are separately liable for the debts of their 
business.)
Salazer and Monie are a partnership.
•
•
•
•
Other forms of business include: 
co-operatives, in which the people 
buying or selling the products 
also share in the profits (such as a 
university co-operative bookstore or 
a farmers’ co-operative) 
incorporated associations, like large 
licensed clubs, which are run like a 
company except that the profits or 
proceeds are used for the benefit of 
the members.
Companies may be: 
private (where shares are offered to 
selected people) 
or
public (in which the shares are 
offered to the public for sale 
through the Australian Stock 
Exchange). Public companies are 
generally large businesses where 
shares are openly traded on the 
stock exchange.

Crazy	John’s:	A	case	study	
Crazy John’s is Australia’s largest mobile 
phone retailer. It is an independently-owned 
company that was founded in 1991 by 
John Ilhan. It now has more than 100 stores 
around Australia and employs over 600 
people.
John Ilhan is one of Australia’s richest people. 
His wealth is estimated to be over $300 
million dollars. John’s family moved from 
Turkey to Melbourne, Australia when he was just three years old. When he started his first Crazy 
John’s mobile phone business in 1991, it was a one-man retail operation based in a small shop in 
the Melbourne suburb of Brunswick. Because he could not afford to carry a large amount of stock, 
he would sign up customers first and then collect the mobile phones from a distributor and deliver 
them to the clients.
So why call it Crazy John’s? The name came from John’s marketing ideas, which at the time were 
considered to be crazy. For example, he was the first one to sell a mobile phone for $1 – other 
companies were charging $200 for a phone. He would give away free accessories just to get the 
business. 
Why was the business so successful? John believes he was in the right place at the right time, 
when the mobile phone market was in its early stages of development. He was also successful in 
positioning the company as a low-cost, high-service, mobile dealership – John says that building 
a reputation for providing quality customer service and competitive prices was an important goal 
from the start. He believes his working class background and lack of formal education did not hold 
him back, as he was able to see opportunities that others might consider too risky.
Today, Crazy John’s is one of the most well  
known brands in Australia and has. It is also the 
largest independent retailer of mobile phones, 
and offers the widest range of phones and 
associated products in Australia. It has strong ties 
with Telstra (being a re-seller of Telstra products) 
and is heavily involved with the world’s top 
mobile phone brands including Nokia, Sony, 
Ericsson, Motorola and Samsung.
4	Crazy	John’s:	A	company	profile
Many businesses start out as small sole traders. But if they are highly successful, they can become 
companies. You don’t have to have a large business to form a company, but there are some 
procedures which must be followed.
FORMING	A	COMPANY
Some important things to remember about a 
company are listed below.
A company is created by law.
It exists in its own right and is separate 
from the owners.
Owners of a company are called 
shareholders.
Liability (debt) is limited to the money 
contributed by shareholders.

John Ilhan has always been concerned 
about the welfare of children, and so in 
2004 he set up The Ilhan Foundation. The 
Foundation gives money to organisations 
which help children in the areas of housing, 
education, family, self development, health 
and medical research.

Mad	Ron’s:	A	case	study
A company’s name is very important in business. 
Sometimes other companies try to cash in on a 
successful company by using a similar name. 
Businessman Ron Bakir founded Crazy Ron’s as a mobile 
phone company. However, his competitor, Crazy 
John’s, sued Bakir’s company in 2003 for trademark 
infringement. Crazy John’s eventually won the court case 
to force Mr Bakir’s business to change its name to Mad 
Ron’s. In 2005, Mad Ron’s was put into liquidation with 
$1.4 million owed to Crazy John’s, the Australian Tax 
Office and others.
Mr Bakir is still paying out creditors from his earlier 
bankruptcy in 2002, when the company formerly known 
as Crazy Ron’s Holdings went broke with personal 
guarantees from Mr Bakir and almost no assets. Most of 
its assets were sold six months earlier to a Bakir-related 
company, according to liquidator Mark Pearce from 
Pearce & Heers.
Some companies, like Mad Ron’s, get into financial difficulties. If the company can’t trade its way 
out of debt, it may be liquidated or wound up. The company’s assets are seized by a liquidator and 
sold to pay the company’s debts.

Going	into	business:	The	steps	involved
Before you start: examine the pros and cons of being a business owner. Consider statistics on 
business failure, know the importance of market research and have an understanding of the 
most common types of business. Know the differences between sole traders, partnerships and 
companies.
Develop a business plan and a marketing plan: get some tips on how to research and write 
these plans.
Plan your finances: work out how you can raise the finance to go into business. Find out 
about financial forecasting, risk management and options for financial assistance. Research tax, 
insurance and superannuation requirements.
Location of your business: consider where to set up your premises to maximise profits, taking 
safety issues into consideration.
Employing staff: understand how to recruit and manage staff, including information about 
legal obligations, dealing with disputes, equal opportunity considerations, health and safety 
in the workplace and ideas for effectively managing staff. Managing the training and skills 
development of staff is very important.
Sales and marketing: learn about market research, your competitors, pricing your product, 
advertising and promotion, public relations, media campaigns, customer relations, payment 
types and sales techniques. Also investigate the importance of brand names and intellectual 
property, copyright and patents.
